INTRODUCTION

Holmes was engaged by Portland Public Schools (PPS) in 2023 to update the seismic assessment information
for each school campus within the district to aid in planning of future projects and bond funding. This initial
assessment is referred to as “Phase 1”. The Phase 1 assessment included 80 total sites and only buildings that
have not been the target of an in-progress retrofit/replacement or a recently completed retrofit. Unreinforced
Masonry (URM) buildings were broken out due to their relatively high risk in order to be prioritized, which
includes 23 sites on the provided URM List and 6 potential additional sites. The data provided by Holmes
includes seismic vulnerabilities, estimated construction costs, and incorporating district-provided information
such as Title 1 designated schools.

In 2024, Holmes was engaged by Portland Public Schools (PPS) to develop a seismic risk ranking system that
will assist the district in planning future projects and bond funding, referred to as “Phase 2”. This project builds
upon the district-wide seismic assessment performed by Holmes in 2024 (referred to as Phase 1, which we've
incorporated into this report to provide a complete reference document). Phase 1 documented the construction
history, identified potential seismic vulnerabilities, and estimated retrofit construction costs for District
buildings.

Seismic risk was evaluated at 75 sites across the District. Schools that have undergone recent seismic retrofits
or are currently scheduled for retrofit or replacement were excluded from the risk ranking assessment. Each
evaluated site had multiple 'Building Parts,' which are different areas of the campus that were identified as
being structurally distinct due to differences in their age, structural systems, or because they are physically
separate buildings.

Each Building Part was assessed individually and assigned its own risk score ranging from 1 to 10, where a high
score indicates that a building type is expected to perform poorly in an earthquake and a low score indicates
that a building type is expected to perform well in an earthquake. The scores are based on a multi-criteria
assessment approach that utilized well-established risk metrics based on building typologies, as well as
building-specific vulnerability information collected in Phase 1 and occupancy data provided by the District.
Additional contextual information such as Title 1A designations and roof replacement priorities was also
incorporated into the assessment documentation.

This report provides an overview of the risk assessment and includes high-level building information for each
campus.

PROJECT OVERVIEW

SEISMIC ASSESSMENT DESCRIPTION

The following steps were performed for each school building:

    1.   Review available existing building documentation.
    2.   Develop a Building Year Plan based on available drawings and/or historic aerial views. Identify
         unreinforced masonry (URM) construction on Plan and approximate square footage of URM areas,
         where occurs.
    3. Develop a list of potential deficiencies. The deficiencies list is informed by the ASCE 41 Tier 1 structural
       checklists for each building type, but are not entirely comprehensive of the Tier 1 methodology.
    4. Perform a site walk to confirm building configurations and identify visible deficiencies and site
       characteristics.
    5. Compile information and develop an engineer’s rough order of magnitude (ROM) pricing. Pricing is
       summarized by URM-only retrofit as well as the complete ROM retrofit for all buildings on the campus.

The assessments utilized FEMA Rapid Visual Screening, ASCE 41 Tier 1 checklists, and Holmes’ experience with
similar building types as a guideline to identify deficiencies. However, these assessments were not a full ASCE
41 Tier 1 assessment, and all deficiencies require further analysis and verification to follow the ASCE 41
methodology. Identification of non-structural deficiencies is outside the scope of this study, however non-
structural deficiencies which may pose a high life-safety hazard (i.e. parapets, masonry chimneys, interior
unreinforced masonry walls) were noted in our assessments. See Figure 1 for more information on typical levels
of seismic assessments compared to the level of assessment completed for this project.

We have assessed and compiled the results for all PPS schools, excluding the following:

    •    Schools currently under design through Modernization & New Construction
    •    Schools with complete or near complete recent seismic upgrades
    •    Schools recently constructed. Individual buildings that comply with the ASCE 41 Chapter 3 design
         years for Benchmark Buildings are also omitted from the assessment and retrofit costs and are noted
         as such in the summary.

SEISMIC RISK ASSESSMENT DESCRIPTION

The seismic risk assessment was designed as a systematic approach to compare the relative risk of buildings
across the District portfolio. As shown in Figure 2, the process begins with establishing the baseline risk using
general, well-established vulnerability information. Individual building scores are then methodically refined by
incorporating building-specific information. This approach ensures that the final risk rankings reflect both
established risk metrics and the unique characteristics of each building in the portfolio, while maintaining
context of other factors that may affect prioritization of retrofits and funding.

A full description of the means and methods used to gather information and determine the risk score is
provided in Appendix A. In general, the assessment of each school followed these key steps:

     1. Establish a Baseline Score for each building based on its structural system and construction year,
        using Hazus Earthquake Loss Estimation Methodology1 developed by the Federal Emergency
        Management Agency (FEMA).
     2. Adjust the Baseline to establish a Building-Specific Score that accounts for building-specific
        information identified in Phase 1 such as completed retrofits and identified deficiencies.
     3. Adjust the Building-Specific Score based on occupancy rates to generate the final Seismic Risk Score
        for each Building Part.
     4. Capture additional contextual information to identify cost-effective retrofit opportunities and inform
        district-wide planning priorities.

Schools Excluded from the Assessment

We have assessed and compiled the results for all PPS schools, excluding the following:

    •     Schools currently under design through Modernization & New Construction
    •     Schools with complete or near complete recent seismic upgrades
    •     Schools recently constructed. Individual buildings that comply with the ASCE 41 Chapter 3 design
          years for Benchmark Buildings are also omitted from the assessment and retrofit costs and are noted
          as such in the summary.
    •     Schools that have been decommissioned or are being leased out for other uses.

RESULTS
The final risk scores as well as the information used for the risk assessment were compiled into a single Excel
document. Information provided in the Excel document can be used by the District to create figures and
analyses that illustrate the relative risk of buildings in the portfolio and support strategic decision-making. For
example, Figure 3 shows the final Seismic Risk Scores of all the evaluated building parts.

The results for each school were also compiled into individual School Seismic Risk Summary pages. The
information presented on these summary pages is defined in Appendix B and the results for each school are
presented in Appendix C.

NEXT STEPS AND RECOMMENDATIONS

We recommend that PPS use the Risk Scores provided in this report as a primary decision-making tool for
allocating seismic upgrade funds. These scores and identified seismic deficiencies should also be integrated
into any future discussions regarding district enrollment changes and facility planning.


RECOMMENDED IMPLEMENTATION APPROACHES

Approach A: Campus-by-Campus Implementation

Under this approach, PPS would prioritize the highest-risk campuses and address all seismic deficiencies
comprehensively at each selected site. This method treats each campus as a complete project, similar to the
district's high school modernization initiatives, where all buildings and building parts receive full seismic
retrofitting or replacement regardless of individual risk scores.

Advantages: This approach maximizes construction efficiency by concentrating resources at fewer locations,
reducing mobilization costs and project management complexity. It ensures complete seismic compliance for
prioritized campuses.

Disadvantages: Funding will be spent on some lower-risk building components within high-risk campuses, and
overall district-wide risk reduction will be limited to fewer sites.

Approach B: Highest-Risk Building Parts

This approach targets individual building parts with the highest risk scores across the district, regardless of
campus location. Implementation would focus on the most critical seismic risk building parts first, while also
considering cost-effective retrofit opportunities (identified within this report) that provide maximum safety
improvement per dollar spent.

Advantages: This method achieves the greatest district-wide risk reduction and protects the largest number of
students by addressing the most dangerous conditions first. It provides more immediate safety improvements
across multiple schools.

Disadvantages: Higher construction mobilization costs due to projects being distributed across numerous
campuses, and increased project management complexity.

IMPLEMENTATION CONSIDERATIONS
Regardless of the chosen approach, we recommend that PPS establish clear criteria for project prioritization
that balances risk scores with practical factors such as available funding, construction feasibility, and
educational continuity requirements.

Pricing Notes
Pricing has been calculated using a ROM (rough order of magnitude) $/SF cost for each building part. The
costs are an engineer’s estimate based on Holmes’ experience with similar projects and only intended for initial
relative budgeting purposes. All costs should be verified by an experienced cost estimator.

URM-Only pricing provided is intended to give an approximate cost estimate to perform a localized URM-Only
retrofit. This price is accompanied by the approximate cost to retrofit all building parts on the campus. The
square footage noted is an approximate boundary for each building part to be retrofitted, and has been
scaled off existing documentation available.

The cost is reflective of the following:
    • Estimates are based on representative cost estimates provided between 2022-2023 (+/-) from
        schematic design retrofit pricing of similar buildings and/or building parts and is a ROUGH order of
        magnitude price. Appropriate contingencies and escalation should be applied.
    • URM-Only retrofits are for seismic upgrades within the URM area indicated in the Building Year Plan.
        While the retrofit will be considered partial (localized only) it is intended to mitigate URM deficiencies
        as well as align with the scope associated with a full seismic upgrade for that building part. For
        example, in addition to bracing of URM walls in the URM-Area-Only, the cost would include items such
        as roof-level seismic, secondary gravity support, and foundation strengthening that would otherwise
        be required as part of a complete seismic upgrade, to avoid remobilization and demolition in the URM
        area.
    • Estimates include consideration of demolition and repair of architectural finishes and MEP as required
        to complete the structural work, per the representative cost estimates provided. They do not include
        costs for improvements/upgrades to these items.
    • Soft costs such as engineering, construction management, additional non-seismic related upgrades,
        and relocation are excluded.

IMPORTANT WARNING: These figures represent preliminary planning estimates ONLY and should NOT be
used for final budgeting or construction decisions. Their primary purpose is to enable RELATIVE comparisons
between building parts/campuses to inform prioritization decisions. Actual construction costs will vary
significantly based on detailed design, market conditions, and site-specific factors not accounted for at this
preliminary stage.

INTRODUCTION

The means and methods used in the seismic risk assessment are described in the following sections. The
process was designed as a systematic approach to compare the relative risk of buildings across the District
portfolio. The assessment of each school followed these key steps:

     1. Establish a Baseline Score for each building based on its structural system and construction year,
        using Hazus Earthquake Loss Estimation Methodology2 developed by the Federal Emergency
        Management Agency (FEMA).
     2. Adjust the Baseline to establish a Building-Specific Score that accounts for building-specific
        information identified in Phase 1 such as completed retrofits and identified deficiencies.
     3. Adjust the Building-Specific Score based on occupancy rates to generate the final Seismic Risk Score
        for each Building Part.
     4. Capture additional contextual information to identify cost-effective retrofit opportunities and inform
        district-wide planning priorities.

This approach ensures that the final risk rankings reflect both established risk metrics and the unique
characteristics of each building in the portfolio, while maintaining context of other factors that may affect
prioritization of retrofits and funding.

BASELINE SCORE

The baseline score is an initial score intended to provide a first pass at understanding the relative seismic risk
of different building types. The baseline score is informed by the Hazus Earthquake Loss Estimation
Methodology which was developed by FEMA and utilizes well established vulnerability and risk metrics for
general building typologies.

The Hazus Methodology is not intended to give building specific information, but rather gives probabilistic risk
information based on site seismicity and basic building information such as the structural system, number of
stories, and year of construction. This Methodology was applied to determine the probability of a building
being in a given damage state and the probability of a building damage causing injuries to occupants.

The baseline score was established by taking the weighted averages of the probability of being in a damage
state and the probability of being in a casualty state. The weighted averages were combined and normalized
between 1 and 9, with a high score indicating that a building type is expected to perform poorly in an
earthquake and a low score indicating that a building type is expected to perform well in an earthquake.




2
 See the Hazus Earthquake Model Technical Manual for more information of the Hazus Earthquake Loss Estimation Methodology:
https://www.fema.gov/sites/default/files/documents/fema_hazus-earthquake-model-technical-manual-6-1.pdf

combinations have been included in the figure to provide a comprehensive view of the data.

Site Seismicity

For the purposes of establishing the baseline score, all sites were assumed to have the same seismicity, and
site-specific geological hazards were not considered. This was considered reasonable because the level of site-
specific soil information varied greatly between campuses. Additionally, the variation of spectral acceleration
values between sites was less than 5%, assuming Site Soil Class D.

Period of Construction

The year of construction was used to identify the appropriate seismic design level designation, which is based
on the building code that was effective at the time of construction and the seismicity of a location. The seismic
design levels for Portland, Oregon were interpreted from information provided in Appendix C of the Hazus
Inventory Technical Manual3 and are summarized in Table 1 below.

Building Type

The Hazus Methodology includes 36 specific building types, which are based on the number of stories and the
classification system described in FEMA 178: NEHRP Handbook for the Seismic Evaluation of Existing Buildings.
In most cases, the Hazus Building Type could be directly interpreted from the description of a building's lateral
force resisting system that was identified in Phase 1.

There were some instances in which judgement had to be used to choose the most appropriate building type
and associated baseline score. Examples of these cases and the decision-making process include the following:

Case 1: Building has more than one lateral force resisting system

    a) If the lateral force resisting systems were URM and another system, the baseline score was the
       weighted average of the two systems based on the URM and Non-URM floor areas reported in Phase 1.

    b) If two or more non-URM lateral force resisting systems were reported, the baseline for the predominant
       system was used. If there was no obvious predominant system, the system that would result in the
       highest baseline was chosen.

Case 2: Building has a lateral force resisting system that does not align with a Hazus building type description

    a) Cold-Formed Steel (CFS) Light Frame Bearing Wall Construction is not included in the Hazus
       classifications. Buildings with CFS bearing walls and sheathed shear walls were assigned the same
       baseline score as Building Type W2 (Wood Frames, Commercial and Industrial). Buildings with CFS
       bearing walls and strap-braced lateral wall systems were assigned the same baseline score as Building
       Type S3 (Steel Light Frame)

    b) Several of the covered play structures have lateral force resisting systems comprised of cantilevered
       wood or steel columns, which is not a building type recognized in the Hazus classification system. The
       baseline score for these structures was therefore assigned manually under the assumption that the
       building type is expected to perform slightly worse than a wood-framed building of the same era.

BUILDING-SPECIFIC SCORE

The Building-Specific Score is an intermediate score between the baseline and final risk scores. This score
includes modfications to the baseline score based on individual building part characteristics but does not yet
include information that reflects the importance of a building part such as occupancy. The Building-Specific
score varies between 0 and 10, with 10 representing the highest relative risk (i.e., the worst expected seismic
performance). This score was determined by adjusting the baseline score for building-specific strengthening
and vulnerability information identified in Phase 1, including completed retrofits and likely deficiencies. The
process for applying retrofit and deficiency adjustments is described below.

Retrofit Adjustment

A retrofit adjustment was applied to buildings in which seismic upgrades had been completed. The adjustment
is intended to reflect the improved seismic performance of these buildings. The seismic upgrades were
categorized as follows:

        Roof-only retrofit (full or partial): Improvements such as parapet strengthening, strengthened
         connections between walls and roofs, reduced chimney height, or other roof-level strengthening.
         These types of retrofits were typically undertaken as part of an increased scope when the building
         was undergoing other improvements such as re-roofing.
        Non-structural seismic upgrades: Improvements that focused on targeted non-structural seismic
         intervention, such as strengthening elements along exit routes and/or bracing a significant amount of
         unreinforced masonry walls.
        Local or targeted seismic upgrades: Improvements that included targeted structural seismic
         interventions, but not a complete retrofit. Example upgrades include providing new shear walls in
         only one direction or strengthening only one portion of the building.
        Full seismic retrofit: Retrofit that complied with ASCE 7 or ASCE 41 standards throughout the
         building.

In general, adjustments for roof-only and non-structural retrofits were relatively small because these are
typically local interventions that, despite providing life-safety performance benefits in moderate earthquakes,
are unlikely to significantly reduce overall damage in a large earthquake. Adjustments for local or targeted
seismic upgrades varied based on the type and extent of the upgrade and were applied on a case-by-case
basis. Buildings that had full seismic strengthening were adjusted so that the baseline would match the
building type and code era for the retrofitted system.

Deficiency Adjustment

Deficiency adjustments were applied to modify the baseline score specifically when buildings exhibited
atypical weaknesses. These adjustments reflect the negative impact of seismic deficiencies identified in Phase 1
that deviate from typical baseline conditions. Each atypical deficiency received a severity rating (insignificant,
minor, moderate, or severe) based on building type. Buildings were then assigned a cumulative deficiency
score calculated from the number and severity of these non-standard deficiencies. This deficiency score was

                                                                         Appendix B: Risk Assessment Means and Methods
                                                                                                   Version 2.0: Aug 2025
                                                                                                            Page B5 of 8
used to systematically reduce the baseline performance rating using an analytical framework based on the
following principles:

        Progressive Amplification: As the deficiencies score increases, the seismic performance
         progressively worsens.
        Baseline-Dependent Sensitivity: Buildings with lower baseline scores show some resilience to minor
         deficiencies but still experience increases when there are severe deficiencies. Buildings with higher
         baseline scores are sensitive to additional deficiencies, with severe deficiencies pushing scores into
         some of the highest risk ratings.
        Graduated Escalation: The framework creates smooth escalation of scores rather than sharp jumps.
         Minor deficiencies may have minimal impact, but moderate-to-severe deficiencies create meaningful
         increases that compound with the baseline score.

BUILDING PART SEISMIC RISK SCORE

The Building Part Seismic Risk Score is the final, reported score and is intended to reflect the relative risk
associated with a building’s seismic performance. The score is determined by adjusting the a Building-Specific
Score based on occupancy, and varies between 0 and 10, with 10 representing the highest relative risk.

Occupancy Adjustment

The occupancy adjustment was applied to reflect the higher risk associated with areas of high occupancy and
lower risk associated with areas of lower occupancy. Occupancy was generalized into three categories:

        High Occupancy: Gym, Cafeteria, Auditorium, Theaters, etc. (assembly areas)
        Typical Occupancy: Classrooms, offices, restrooms, locker rooms, etc.
        Low Occupancy: Maintenance, utility, kitchen, storage, etc. (back of house areas)

Buildings received a positive occupancy adjustment (risk score increased) based on the amount of building
area associated with high occupancy and a negative occupancy adjustment (risk score decreased) based on
the amount of building area associated with low occupancy. No adjustment was applied for areas of typical
occupancy.

                                                                                                  Version 2.0: Aug 2025
                                                                                                           Page B6 of 8
BUILDING SCORES SUMMARY

Figure A1 shows the range of seismic risk scores for the buildings considered in this assessment. The highest
scores were generally associated with pre-code unreinforced masonry and pre-cast concrete tilt up
construction. Pre-code concrete shear wall and reinforced masonry also tended to score relatively high.
Modern buildngs, particularly those of wood framed construction, typically had the lowest scores.




                    Figure A1. Seismic Risk Scores of all building parts assessed




                                                                         Appendix B: Risk Assessment Means and Methods
                                                                                                   Version 2.0: Aug 2025
                                                                                                            Page B7 of 8
COST INFORMATION AND VALUE FOR MONEY OPPORTUNITIES

Rough Order of Magnitude Retrofit Cost

Pricing was calculated in Phase 1 using a ROM (rough order of magnitude) $/SF cost for each building part,
based on similar construction estimates using 2023 dollars.

The costs are an engineer’s estimate based on Holmes’ experience with similar projects and only intended for
initial relative budgeting purposes. All project specific costs should be verified by an experienced cost
estimator based on a more in-depth seismic strengthening scheme. URM-Only pricing provided is intended to
give an approximate cost estimate to perform a localized URM-Only retrofit. This price is accompanied by the
approximate cost to retrofit all building parts on the campus. The square footage noted is an approximate
boundary for each building part to be retrofitted and has been scaled off existing documentation available.

Further information about the provided ROM pricing is available in the Phase 1 report.

Opportunity to coordinate with roof replacement

Coordinating seismic upgrades with roof replacements can significantly reduce construction costs and
minimize downtime. PPS provided the 2024 Roof Assessment Report by Professional Roof Consultants, Inc.,
which presents a detailed evaluation of roof systems across all District buildings and includes a prioritization
system for roof replacement (described in Figure 3).




                             Figure 3. 2024 Roof Assessment Priority System

To facilitate coordination between roof work and seismic interventions, roof replacement priorities have been
reported for each campus. However, the roof area designations in the Roof Assessment Report do not align
with the building part designations used in Phase 1 of this study. Therefore, readers should compare the roof
plans provided in the 2024 Roof Assessment Report with the building year plans in this study to identify specific
areas where roof replacement and roof-level seismic upgrades can be effectively coordinated.

Low cost + high safety return projects

Each building was reviewed to identify any retrofit opportunities that would be good value for money. That is,
there is a localized and relatively low cost retrofit that would have high safety returns. For example, a high
occupancy area such as a gym or cafeteria with one or more URM walls would fit into this category.
